title: Exam P — Probability
subtitle: Build probability into a reflex. Every concept is taught to the point where the SOA question feels like recognizing an old friend.
intro: This is not a formula sheet with a pulse. Each concept walks the same arc — the stakes, the plain-language intuition before any symbol, the formula, a fully worked SOA-style example, a speed trick, the exact trap that catches most students, an interactive sim where it helps, and active-recall cards. Then a timed mastery gate decides whether it has actually stuck. Miss the bar and the concept resurfaces on a spaced schedule until recall is automatic. Probability rewards pattern recognition under time pressure — so we drill the patterns until they are reflexes.

format.passing: Grade 6 or higher on the SOA 0–10 scale — roughly 70% of questions correct. You get 3 hours for 30 questions, so about 6 minutes each, but the easy ones should take 90 seconds so you can spend 8+ on the hard ones.

modules.title: General Probability
modules.blurb: Sample spaces, the axioms, counting, conditional probability, Bayes, and independence. This is the grammar of the entire exam — every later topic is built on it, and roughly a quarter of your questions live right here.

concepts.title: Sample Spaces & Events
concepts.tagline: Every probability question is secretly a set question. Learn to see the sets and half the work disappears.

sections.body: Before you can compute a probability you have to know **what you are counting over**. Get the sample space wrong and every later step is exactly wrong. Most missed P questions are not algebra mistakes — they are set-up mistakes made in the first ten seconds.

sections.title: Think of it as a room of outcomes
sections.body: The **sample space** $S$ is the complete list of everything that could happen — the whole room. An **event** is any group of those outcomes — a roped-off section of the room. Probability is just *what fraction of the room* an event occupies (when outcomes are equally likely). Union $A \cup B$ = in either section. Intersection $A \cap B$ = in both at once. Complement $A^c$ = everything outside the section. That is the entire vocabulary.

sections.title: The identities you actually reuse
sections.body: Inclusion–exclusion: $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$ Complement: $$P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$$ De Morgan, the most under-used pair on the exam: $$(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c, \qquad (A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c$$

sections.title: Inclusion–exclusion in the wild
sections.body: In a group, $P(\text{coffee}) = 0.7$, $P(\text{tea}) = 0.5$, and $P(\text{both}) = 0.3$. Find the probability a person drinks **neither**.
steps: Drinks at least one: $P(C \cup T) = 0.7 + 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.9$.
Neither is the complement of at least one: $P((C \cup T)^c) = 1 - 0.9$.

sections.title: Inclusion–exclusion for three events
sections.body: A student is enrolled in Math, Physics, and Chemistry with $P(M)=0.5$, $P(P)=0.4$, $P(C)=0.3$, $P(M\cap P)=0.2$, $P(M\cap C)=0.15$, $P(P\cap C)=0.1$, and $P(M\cap P\cap C)=0.05$. Find the probability the student takes **at least one** of the three.
steps: The three-event version adds back the triple overlap that the pairwise subtractions remove twice: $P(M\cup P\cup C) = \sum P(\text{singles}) - \sum P(\text{pairs}) + P(\text{triple})$.
Cross-check the alternating sign pattern (+singles, −pairs, +triple): each region of the Venn diagram is now counted exactly once. So $P(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20$.

sections.title: Draw the two-circle Venn, fill the middle first
sections.body: Always place $P(A \cap B)$ in the overlap **first**, then subtract it from each circle so the *only-A* and *only-B* regions are correct. Once the three regions and the outside sum to 1, you can read off any compound probability by eye — no formula recall under pressure.

sections.title: Adding probabilities that overlap
sections.body: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ is **only** true when $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive (no overlap). If they can both happen, you double-count the middle. When a problem says *or* and the events can co-occur, you must subtract $P(A \cap B)$. Forgetting this single subtraction is the most common General-Probability error.

cards.front: Why does inclusion–exclusion subtract $P(A\cap B)$ — and why add the triple back for three events?
cards.back: Adding $P(A)+P(B)$ counts the overlap twice, so you subtract it once to count each outcome exactly once. With three events the pairwise subtractions remove the central triple-overlap region too many times, so you add $P(A\cap B\cap C)$ back to restore it. It is all bookkeeping to count every region precisely once.

cards.front: Why is De Morgan a probability shortcut, not just set algebra?
cards.back: It converts a complement of a union into an intersection (and vice versa). A 'neither' question — $(A\cup B)^c$ — becomes $A^c\cap B^c$, which is often far easier to compute directly. Whenever 'at least one' is awkward, complement it and let De Morgan flip the and/or so the easy quantity is exposed.

questions.q: If $P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.5$, and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$, what is $P(A \cap B)$?
questions.explain: Rearrange inclusion–exclusion: $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.8 = 0.3$.

questions.q: Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.3$, and they are mutually exclusive. What is $P(A^c \cap B^c)$?
questions.explain: By De Morgan, $P(A^c \cap B^c) = P((A \cup B)^c) = 1 - P(A \cup B)$. Mutually exclusive means $P(A \cup B) = 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7$, so the answer is $1 - 0.7 = 0.30$.

questions.q: A survey finds $P(\text{news}) = 0.55$, $P(\text{sports}) = 0.45$, and $P(\text{neither}) = 0.20$. What fraction read both?
Which statement is always true for any two events?
questions.explain: A union can only add outcomes, so $P(A \cup B) \ge P(A)$ always. The intersection is a subset of $A$, so it is $\le P(A)$. The additive and multiplicative identities need extra conditions (mutual exclusivity, independence).

questions.q: If $P(A \cup B) = 0.9$, $P(A) = 0.5$, and $A,B$ are independent, find $P(B)$.
questions.explain: Independence gives $P(A \cap B) = 0.5\,P(B)$. Inclusion–exclusion: $0.9 = 0.5 + P(B) - 0.5P(B) = 0.5 + 0.5P(B)$, so $0.5P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.8$.

concepts.title: Counting & the Axioms
concepts.tagline: Permutations vs combinations decided by one question: does order matter? Get that reflex and counting problems stop being scary.

sections.body: When outcomes are equally likely, probability collapses to **counting**: favorable over total. The entire difficulty is counting correctly — and 90% of that is one decision: *does order matter?*

sections.title: Order matters → permutation. Order does not → combination.
sections.body: Picking a **president, VP, treasurer** from a club: order matters, the roles are different — that is a permutation. Picking a **committee of 3**: order does not matter, a group is a group — that is a combination. The number of combinations is always smaller, because you stop counting the same group in different seat orders.

sections.title: The three counting tools
sections.body: Multiplication rule: independent stages multiply. Permutations of $k$ from $n$: $$P(n,k) = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$$ Combinations of $k$ from $n$: $$\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$$ The three Kolmogorov axioms everything rests on: $P(A) \ge 0$, $P(S) = 1$, and for disjoint events $P(\bigcup A_i) = \sum P(A_i)$.

sections.title: A classic equally-likely count
sections.body: From a standard deck, draw 5 cards. What is the probability of exactly 2 aces?
steps: Total hands: $\binom{52}{5}$.
Choose 2 of the 4 aces: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$.
Choose the other 3 cards from the 48 non-aces: $\binom{48}{3}$.
Probability $= \dfrac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{3}}{\binom{52}{5}} = \dfrac{6 \cdot 17296}{2598960} \approx 0.0399$.

sections.title: When order matters: an offices problem
sections.body: A club of 8 members elects a president, a vice-president, and a treasurer — three *distinct* offices, one person each. In how many ways can the slate be filled, and what is the probability that a particular member, Ann, holds one of the three offices?
steps: Order matters here (the roles differ), so use a permutation: $P(8,3) = 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 = 336$ possible slates.
Count the slates where Ann holds an office: she can take any of the 3 roles, and the remaining 2 roles are filled from the other 7: $3 \cdot P(7,2) = 3 \cdot (7 \cdot 6) = 126$.
Probability $= \dfrac{126}{336} = 0.375$.
Cross-check via the complement: $P(\text{Ann gets nothing}) = \dfrac{P(7,3)}{P(8,3)} = \dfrac{7\cdot 6\cdot 5}{8\cdot 7\cdot 6} = \dfrac{210}{336} = 0.625$, and $1 - 0.625 = 0.375$. ✓

sections.title: Build the count as choose-this-then-that
sections.body: Every hypergeometric-style count is *choose the good ones $\times$ choose the rest, over choose everything*. Write the denominator first ($\binom{N}{n}$ — choose your whole sample), then split the numerator into the groups the problem cares about. The structure writes itself.

sections.title: Using a permutation when order is irrelevant
sections.body: If you count a 3-person committee with $P(n,3)$ instead of $\binom{n}{3}$, you over-count by $3! = 6$. The tell: if swapping two chosen items gives a *different* outcome you care about, order matters; if it gives the *same* outcome, divide out the $k!$.

cards.front: Why is the permutation count exactly $k!$ times the combination count?
cards.back: A combination is an unordered group of $k$; a permutation is that same group with the seating order tracked. Each group of $k$ can be arranged in $k!$ orders, so $P(n,k) = \binom{n}{k}\cdot k!$. That is also *why* combinations are always smaller — they collapse all $k!$ orderings of a group into one count.

cards.front: Why does an equally-likely probability reduce to a counting ratio, and what do the axioms guarantee?
cards.back: If every outcome in $S$ is equally likely, the axiom $P(S)=1$ spreads the total mass evenly, so each outcome carries weight $1/|S|$ and an event's probability is just (favorable)/(total). Non-negativity and additivity for disjoint events then guarantee those counts combine consistently — no probability is negative and disjoint pieces simply add.

questions.q: How many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 10 people?
How many distinct 4-letter arrangements use the letters of the word $\textbf{BOOK}$?
questions.explain: There are $4!$ arrangements but the two O's are identical, so divide by $2!$: $24/2 = 12$.

questions.q: A box has 6 red and 4 blue balls. Drawing 3 without replacement, what is $P(\text{all red})$?
A 4-digit PIN allows digits 0–9 with repetition. How many PINs have no two adjacent digits equal?
questions.explain: First digit: 10 choices. Each later digit just needs to differ from the one immediately before it: 9 choices each. So $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 9 \cdot 9 = 10\cdot 9^3$.

questions.q: From 5 men and 4 women, a committee of 4 with exactly 2 women is formed. How many committees?
questions.explain: Choose 2 of 4 women and 2 of 5 men: $\binom{4}{2}\binom{5}{2} = 6 \cdot 10 = 60$.

concepts.title: Conditional Probability
concepts.tagline: New information shrinks the room. Conditioning is just zooming the sample space into the part you now know is true.

sections.body: Almost every hard P question hides a *given that* — and the moment you condition, you are working in a **smaller world**. Students who picture that shrinking world get these right fast; students who memorize the formula blind get tangled in which probability goes on the bottom.

sections.title: Conditioning = restrict, then renormalize
sections.body: $P(A \mid B)$ asks: *given we already landed inside $B$, how much of $B$ is also $A$?* You throw away everything outside $B$ (the new world is $B$), then ask what fraction of that world is $A \cap B$. That is why $B$ sits in the denominator — it is the new total.

sections.title: Definition, multiplication, total probability
sections.body: Definition: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \quad P(B) > 0$$ Multiplication rule (rearranged): $$P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)$$ Law of total probability over a partition $B_1,\dots,B_n$: $$P(A) = \sum_i P(A \mid B_i)\,P(B_i)$$

sections.title: Total probability across two factories
sections.body: Factory 1 makes 60% of units at a 2% defect rate; Factory 2 makes 40% at a 5% defect rate. What fraction of all units are defective?
steps: Condition on factory: $P(D) = P(D\mid F_1)P(F_1) + P(D\mid F_2)P(F_2)$.

sections.title: The multiplication rule in sequence (no replacement)
sections.body: An urn holds 5 red and 3 blue balls. You draw two balls *without replacement*. What is the probability both are red?
steps: Chain the draws with the multiplication rule: $P(R_1 \cap R_2) = P(R_1)\,P(R_2 \mid R_1)$.
First draw: $P(R_1) = 5/8$. After a red is removed, 4 reds remain of 7 balls, so $P(R_2 \mid R_1) = 4/7$ — conditioning *shrinks the world* from 8 balls to 7.
Multiply along the path: $\dfrac{5}{8}\cdot\dfrac{4}{7} = \dfrac{20}{56} = \dfrac{5}{14} \approx 0.357$.
Cross-check by counting unordered pairs: $\dfrac{\binom{5}{2}}{\binom{8}{2}} = \dfrac{10}{28} = \dfrac{5}{14}$ — the conditioning chain and the count agree. ✓

sections.title: The tree: branch probabilities multiply along a path
sections.body: Draw a tree: first branch on the condition ($F_1$ vs $F_2$), then on the outcome (defect vs not). The probability of any leaf is the **product** along its path. To get a marginal like $P(D)$, **add** every leaf where $D$ happens. Multiply along, add across — that single rule solves most conditional problems without algebra.

sections.title: Flipping the condition
sections.body: $P(A \mid B) \ne P(B \mid A)$ in general. *The probability a defective part came from Factory 2* is **not** the same as *the defect rate at Factory 2*. Confusing these two directions is the single biggest conditional-probability mistake — and it is exactly what Bayes' theorem exists to fix.

cards.front: Why does $P(B)$ sit in the denominator of $P(A\mid B)$, and why does the law of total probability work?
cards.back: Conditioning makes $B$ the entire new world, so you renormalize by $P(B)$ — the size of that new total — and keep only the $A\cap B$ slice. The law of total probability runs this in reverse: split $S$ into disjoint conditions $B_i$, find $A$'s share inside each, and weight by how likely each $B_i$ is. Every outcome of $A$ lives in exactly one $B_i$, so the weighted pieces reassemble the whole.

cards.front: Why is $P(A\mid B)$ generally not equal to $P(B\mid A)$?
cards.back: They divide the *same* overlap $P(A\cap B)$ by *different* totals — one by $P(B)$, the other by $P(A)$. 'The chance a defective part came from Factory 2' (condition on defective) is a different world than 'Factory 2's defect rate' (condition on Factory 2). Swapping the two is the classic error Bayes' theorem exists to correct.

questions.q: $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. Find $P(A \mid B)$.
An urn has 3 red and 2 green balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Given the first is red, what is the probability the second is red?
questions.explain: After removing one red, 2 red and 2 green remain, so $P(\text{2nd red}\mid\text{1st red}) = \frac{2}{4} = 0.5$.

questions.q: 30% of emails are spam. 90% of spam and 5% of non-spam contain the word 'free'. What fraction of all emails contain 'free'?
If $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(A \mid B) = 0.5$, what is $P(A \cup B)$?
questions.explain: $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ means independence, so $P(A\cap B)=0.5\cdot0.4=0.2$. Then $P(A\cup B)=0.5+0.4-0.2=0.7$.

questions.q: A test for a condition is taken in two independent stages; the second is taken only if the first is positive. $P(\text{1st}+)=0.2$ and $P(\text{2nd}+\mid\text{1st}+)=0.6$. What is $P(\text{both}+)$?

concepts.title: Bayes' Theorem
concepts.tagline: Reverse the conditional. The reason a 99%-accurate test can still be wrong most of the time — and why this is a probability superpower.

sections.body: A disease hits 1 in 100 people. A test is 99% accurate both ways. You test positive. Most people — including doctors — guess your chance of being sick is about 99%. **It is roughly 50%.** Bayes is the tool that makes that counterintuitive truth obvious, and the SOA loves it.

sections.title: Rare causes stay rare even after evidence
sections.body: The base rate dominates. If almost nobody has the disease, then the *false positives drawn from the huge healthy crowd* can rival or outnumber the *true positives from the tiny sick group*. Bayes simply weighs each path by how many people actually walk it. Always think in **counts of people**, not floating probabilities.

sections.title: Bayes' theorem
sections.body: $$P(B_k \mid A) = \frac{P(A \mid B_k)\,P(B_k)}{\sum_i P(A \mid B_i)\,P(B_i)}$$ The numerator is one path; the denominator is the law of total probability — *all* the paths that produce the evidence $A$. The whole theorem is: this path's weight divided by every path's weight.

widget.caption: Set prevalence to 1%, sensitivity and specificity to 99% each, and watch the posterior land near 50% — the false positives from the healthy majority swamp the true positives. Then push prevalence up and watch the posterior climb.

sections.title: The 99% test, by counting people
sections.body: Prevalence 1%, sensitivity 99%, specificity 99%. You test positive — find $P(\text{disease} \mid +)$.
steps: Imagine 10,000 people. Diseased: $100$. Healthy: $9{,}900$.
True positives: $99\% \times 100 = 99$.
False positives: $1\% \times 9{,}900 = 99$.

sections.title: Reversing the conditional: which factory?
sections.body: Recall the factories: Factory 1 makes 60% of units at a 2% defect rate; Factory 2 makes 40% at a 5% defect rate, so the overall defect rate is $0.032$. A unit is found **defective** — what is the probability it came from Factory 2?
steps: Bayes flips the known direction (defect rate *given* factory) into the wanted one (factory *given* defective): $P(F_2 \mid D) = \dfrac{P(D\mid F_2)P(F_2)}{P(D)}$.
Numerator — the $F_2$ path: $P(D\mid F_2)P(F_2) = (0.05)(0.4) = 0.020$.
Denominator — every path that yields a defect (the total probability we already found): $P(D) = 0.032$.

Cross-check: the other path gives $P(F_1\mid D) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375$, and $0.625 + 0.375 = 1$. The posteriors over all causes must sum to 1. ✓ Notice Factory 2 supplies only 40% of units but 62.5% of the defects — the evidence shifted the odds toward the riskier source.

sections.title: Skip the formula — use a population of 10,000
sections.body: Never plug into the Bayes fraction cold under time pressure. Pick a round population (10,000 or 100,000), split it by the base rate, then apply the rates to get integer counts in each cell. The answer is *favorable count / total positive count*. Faster, and you literally cannot flip the conditional by accident.

sections.title: Ignoring the base rate
sections.body: The base-rate fallacy: jumping from *the test is 99% accurate* to *I am 99% likely sick*. That throws away $P(B_k)$, the prior. When a condition is rare, even an excellent test produces a flood of false positives. The prior is never optional — it is half the calculation.

cards.front: Why is the denominator of Bayes the *sum over every cause path*, not just the one you care about?
cards.back: The posterior is this cause's share of the evidence, so the denominator must be the total weight of evidence from *all* causes: $\sum_i P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i)$. That total is exactly the law of total probability. Dividing one path by the sum of all paths is what forces the posteriors over the causes to add to 1.

cards.front: Why can a 99%-accurate test still leave you only ~50% likely to be sick?
cards.back: Because the posterior weighs each path by how many people actually walk it. With a rare disease, the 1% of false positives drawn from the *huge* healthy crowd can equal the true positives from the *tiny* sick group. The prior (base rate) is half the calculation — drop it and you commit the base-rate fallacy.

questions.q: A factory's machines A and B make 70% and 30% of output, with defect rates 2% and 6%. A defective item is found. What is $P(\text{from B} \mid \text{defective})$?
questions.explain: Defects: A contributes $0.02\times0.7=0.014$; B contributes $0.06\times0.3=0.018$. Posterior for B $= \frac{0.018}{0.014+0.018}=\frac{0.018}{0.032}=0.5625\approx0.56$.

questions.q: Disease prevalence 2%. Sensitivity 95%, specificity 90%. Given a positive test, $P(\text{disease}\mid +)$ is closest to:
questions.explain: Per 10,000: diseased 200, healthy 9,800. True positives $0.95\times200=190$. False positives $0.10\times9{,}800=980$. $\frac{190}{190+980}=\frac{190}{1170}\approx0.162$.

questions.q: Two urns: Urn 1 has 2 red, 3 white; Urn 2 has 4 red, 1 white. An urn is picked at random and a red ball drawn. What is $P(\text{Urn 1}\mid \text{red})$?
An insurer classifies drivers as low (60%, claim prob 0.05) or high risk (40%, claim prob 0.20). Given a driver filed a claim, what is the probability they are high risk?
questions.explain: Claim mass: low $0.6\times0.05=0.03$; high $0.4\times0.20=0.08$. Posterior high $=\frac{0.08}{0.03+0.08}=\frac{0.08}{0.11}\approx0.727$.

questions.q: In Bayes' theorem, increasing the prior $P(B_k)$ while holding the likelihoods fixed will:
questions.explain: A larger prior puts more weight on that cause's path in both numerator and denominator, but the net effect raises its posterior share. Priors and posteriors move together when likelihoods are fixed.

concepts.title: Independence
concepts.tagline: The most abused word on the exam. Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive — confusing them costs easy points.

sections.body: Independence lets you **multiply** — it turns hard joint probabilities into easy products. But it is constantly confused with mutual exclusivity, which is almost its opposite. Nailing the distinction is free points.

sections.title: Independent = no information; exclusive = total information
sections.body: **Independent**: learning $B$ happened tells you *nothing* about $A$ — coin flips. **Mutually exclusive**: learning $B$ happened tells you $A$ *definitely did not* — they cannot co-occur. Far from being the same, mutually exclusive events (with positive probability) are *strongly dependent*: one happening rules the other out.

sections.title: The two definitions, side by side
sections.body: Independent: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B) \iff P(A \mid B) = P(A)$$ Mutually exclusive: $$P(A \cap B) = 0$$ For $n$ independent events the joint factorizes: $P(A_1 \cap \cdots \cap A_n) = \prod_i P(A_i)$.

sections.title: At least one success
sections.body: Three independent components each work with probability 0.9. Find the probability at least one works.
steps: Complement is cleaner: at least one $= 1 - P(\text{none work})$.
All fail (independent): $P(\text{none}) = 0.1^3 = 0.001$.
So $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.001 = 0.999$.

sections.title: Testing whether two events are independent
sections.body: You are told $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$, and $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?
steps: Independence is a *checkable equation*, not a story — first recover the overlap. Inclusion–exclusion: $P(A\cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cup B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.7 = 0.2$.
Compare to the independence benchmark $P(A)P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.20$.
The actual overlap $0.2$ equals the product $0.20$, so **yes, $A$ and $B$ are independent**.
Cross-check through the conditional form: $P(A\mid B) = \dfrac{0.2}{0.4} = 0.5 = P(A)$ — knowing $B$ leaves $A$'s probability unchanged, the defining signature of independence. ✓

sections.title: 'At least one' → take the complement
sections.body: Whenever you see *at least one*, do not sum the messy cases — compute $1 - P(\text{none})$. With independence, $P(\text{none})$ is just a clean product of the individual failure probabilities. This complement move shows up on the exam constantly.

sections.title: Treating mutually exclusive as independent
sections.body: If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability, they are **dependent** — because $P(A \mid B) = 0 \ne P(A)$. So you cannot multiply their probabilities. Two events can be independent, or mutually exclusive, but (with positive probability) never both.

cards.front: Why are 'independent' and 'mutually exclusive' nearly opposites, not synonyms?
cards.back: Independent means $B$ tells you *nothing* about $A$ ($P(A\mid B)=P(A)$). Mutually exclusive means $B$ tells you *everything* — $A$ definitely didn't happen ($P(A\mid B)=0$). So two positive-probability events can be one or the other but never both: exclusivity is a strong form of dependence.

cards.front: Why is the complement the right move for 'at least one' under independence?
cards.back: 'At least one' spans many messy overlapping cases, but its complement — 'none' — is a single clean event. With independence the events don't interact, so $P(\text{none})$ factors into a simple product of each failure probability, and $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - \prod P(\text{fail}_i)$. One subtraction replaces a sum over many cases.

questions.q: Two independent events have $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.4$. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
A system has 4 independent components each failing with probability 0.2. What is the probability the system survives (all work)?
questions.explain: Each works with prob 0.8; all four: $0.8^4 = 0.4096 \approx 0.41$.

questions.q: Events $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive with $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(A \mid B)$?
questions.explain: Mutually exclusive means $A$ cannot occur when $B$ does, so $P(A\mid B)=0$. This is why they are dependent, not independent.

questions.q: A fair coin is flipped 5 times. What is the probability of at least one head?
$A$, $B$, $C$ are independent with probabilities 0.5, 0.6, 0.7. Find $P(\text{exactly one occurs})$ ... closest value:

modules.title: Univariate Random Variables
modules.blurb: The biggest slice of the exam by far — nearly half your questions. Distributions, expectation and variance, the named discrete and continuous families, and moment generating functions. Master this module and you have mastered most of Exam P.

concepts.title: Random Variables, PMFs, PDFs & CDFs
concepts.tagline: A distribution is just a way of spreading 1 unit of probability over the number line. Discrete sprinkles it; continuous spreads it.

sections.body: Half the exam lives on top of one idea: a random variable carries a **total of 1** unit of probability, and a distribution describes exactly how that 1 is spread. Once you see every pmf and pdf as *the same single unit, distributed differently*, the named families stop being memorization.

sections.title: Discrete sprinkles, continuous spreads
sections.body: A **discrete** variable drops chunks of probability on specific points — the heights $p(x)$ are actual probabilities and must sum to 1. A **continuous** variable smears probability like butter; the height $f(x)$ is a *density*, not a probability, and you get probability only by integrating over an interval (an *area*). For a continuous variable, $P(X = x) = 0$ — a single point has no width, hence no area.

sections.title: The three functions and how they connect
sections.body: Discrete pmf sums to 1: $\sum_x p(x) = 1$. Continuous pdf integrates to 1: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1$. The CDF accumulates probability up to a point: $$F(x) = P(X \le x)$$ For continuous $X$, density is the derivative of the CDF: $f(x) = F'(x)$, and $P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$.

widget.caption: Switch between Binomial, Poisson, Geometric, Normal, and Exponential. Drag the parameters and watch the shape — and the mean and variance — respond. Build the visual memory now; it pays off on every distribution question.

sections.title: Find the constant, then a probability
sections.body: Let $f(x) = c x^2$ for $0 \le x \le 2$ and 0 elsewhere. Find $c$, then $P(X \le 1)$.
steps: Total area is 1: $\int_0^2 c x^2\,dx = c\cdot \frac{x^3}{3}\Big|_0^2 = c\cdot\frac{8}{3} = 1$.

sections.title: From CDF back to density
sections.body: A continuous variable has CDF $F(x) = x^2$ for $0 \le x \le 1$ (and $0$ below, $1$ above). Find the density $f(x)$ and the probability $P(0.2 \le X \le 0.5)$.
steps: Density is the *slope* of the accumulated probability: $f(x) = F'(x) = 2x$ on $[0,1]$.
Sanity-check it is a valid pdf: $f(x) = 2x \ge 0$ on $[0,1]$, and $\int_0^1 2x\,dx = x^2\big|_0^1 = 1$. ✓
Probability over an interval is just the jump in the CDF: $P(0.2 \le X \le 0.5) = F(0.5) - F(0.2) = 0.25 - 0.04 = 0.21$.
Cross-check by integrating the density: $\int_{0.2}^{0.5} 2x\,dx = x^2\big|_{0.2}^{0.5} = 0.25 - 0.04 = 0.21$ — differentiating then re-integrating returns the same answer. ✓

sections.title: First move on any pdf: set the area to 1
sections.body: Whenever a density has an unknown constant, your first line is always $\int f = 1$ — that single equation solves for the constant. And to get any probability, integrate the density (or subtract two CDF values). Density questions are integration questions in disguise.

sections.title: Reading a density as a probability
sections.body: $f(x)$ can exceed 1 — it is a density, not a probability. A narrow tall pdf can have $f(x) = 5$ and still integrate to 1. Never write $P(X = a) = f(a)$ for a continuous variable; that probability is 0. Probability is always an *area* under $f$, never a height.

cards.front: Why can a density $f(x)$ exceed 1 while a pmf $p(x)$ never can?
cards.back: A pmf value *is* a probability, so it lives in $[0,1]$ and the values sum to 1. A pdf value is a *density* — probability per unit length — so it only has to integrate to 1. A tall narrow pdf can hit $f(x)=5$ over a width of $0.1$ and still enclose area 1. Probability is the area under $f$, never its height, which is why $P(X=a)=0$ for continuous $X$.

cards.front: How do the pdf and CDF connect, and why does $P(a\le X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$?
cards.back: The CDF accumulates probability up to a point, $F(x)=P(X\le x)$, so the density is its slope: $f(x)=F'(x)$. Probability on $[a,b]$ is the *amount accumulated by $b$ minus the amount already accumulated by $a$* — i.e. $F(b)-F(a)$ — which by the fundamental theorem of calculus equals $\int_a^b f$.

questions.q: A pdf is $f(x) = kx$ for $0 \le x \le 4$. Find $k$.
A CDF is $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/2}$ for $x \ge 0$. Find $P(1 \le X \le 3)$.
Which of the following must always hold for a continuous pdf?
questions.explain: A pdf must be non-negative and integrate to 1. It may exceed 1, it need not be monotonic, and point probabilities are zero.

questions.q: A discrete RV has $P(X=k) = c/2^k$ for $k = 1,2,3,\dots$. Find $c$.

concepts.title: Expectation & Variance
concepts.tagline: The center and the spread. Plus the one shortcut — Var = E[X²] − (E[X])² — that you will use on a third of the exam.

sections.body: Expectation is the long-run average; variance is how violently outcomes scatter around it. Together they summarize a distribution in two numbers — and the SOA asks for one or both on a huge share of questions. The computational shortcut below is non-negotiable to memorize.

sections.title: Balance point and spread
sections.body: $E[X]$ is the **balance point** of the distribution — where the probability mass would teeter on a fulcrum. Variance measures the *average squared distance* from that balance point: small variance means tightly clustered, large variance means wild. We square the distances so positives and negatives do not cancel; the standard deviation un-squares it back to the original units.

sections.title: Definitions and the shortcut
sections.body: Expectation: $E[X] = \sum_x x\,p(x)$ or $\int x f(x)\,dx$. Law of the unconscious statistician: $E[g(X)] = \sum g(x)p(x)$ or $\int g(x)f(x)\,dx$. The variance shortcut: $$\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$$ Linearity, always true: $E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b$ and $\mathrm{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

sections.title: Mean and variance of a small die-like RV
sections.body: $X$ takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

sections.title: Continuous mean, variance, and a linear transform
sections.body: A continuous variable has density $f(x) = 2x$ on $[0,1]$. Find $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$, then use them to get $\mathrm{Var}(2X + 5)$ without re-integrating.
steps: Mean by LOTUS: $E[X] = \int_0^1 x\cdot 2x\,dx = \int_0^1 2x^2\,dx = \tfrac{2}{3}$.
Second moment, same machinery: $E[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2\cdot 2x\,dx = \int_0^1 2x^3\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

Variance via the shortcut, *not* by integrating squared deviations: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} - \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{4}{9} = \tfrac{1}{18} \approx 0.0556$.

Linear transform: the shift $+5$ contributes nothing and the scale $2$ enters squared, so $\mathrm{Var}(2X+5) = 2^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{18} = \tfrac{2}{9} \approx 0.222$. (As a check, the mean *does* move: $E[2X+5] = 2(\tfrac23)+5 = \tfrac{19}{3}$.)

sections.title: Never integrate variance directly
sections.body: Computing $\int (x - \mu)^2 f(x)\,dx$ by hand is slow and error-prone. Always use $\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - \mu^2$: find $E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$ with the same machinery, then subtract. And remember the constant $b$ vanishes from variance — only the scale $a$ survives, squared.

sections.title: Forgetting to square the scalar in variance
sections.body: $\mathrm{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$, **not** $a\,\mathrm{Var}(X)$, and the $+b$ contributes nothing. Doubling a random variable quadruples its variance. Equally common: $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y) \ne \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)$ unless $X$ and $Y$ are uncorrelated.

cards.front: Why does $\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$, and why prefer it to integrating squared deviations?
cards.back: Expand the definition: $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=E[X^2-2\mu X+\mu^2]=E[X^2]-2\mu E[X]+\mu^2=E[X^2]-\mu^2$. So the two forms are *identical* — but $E[X^2]$ uses the same summation/integration machinery as $E[X]$, so you compute two ordinary moments and subtract, instead of doing the messy $(x-\mu)^2$ integral.

cards.front: Why does $\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$ — the shift gone, the scale squared?
cards.back: Variance measures spread around the mean, and sliding the whole distribution by $b$ moves the mean with it, leaving every distance from center unchanged — so $b$ drops out. Scaling by $a$ stretches each deviation by $a$; since variance averages *squared* deviations, that scales it by $a^2$. (Hence doubling a variable quadruples its variance.)

questions.q: $X$ has $E[X] = 3$ and $E[X^2] = 13$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
If $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 5$, what is $\mathrm{Var}(3X - 2)$?
For $f(x) = 2x$ on $[0,1]$, find $E[X]$.
$X$ has mean 10 and variance 4. Define $Y = 2X + 5$. Find $E[Y]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)$.
An insurance loss $X$ has $E[X]=500$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=10000$. The insurer pays $0.8X$. What is the standard deviation of the payment?

concepts.title: The Discrete Families
concepts.tagline: Binomial, Poisson, geometric, negative binomial, hypergeometric — recognize the story and the formula is automatic.

sections.body: You will not derive distributions on the exam — you will **recognize** them. Each named discrete family is a story: counting successes, counting trials until success, counting rare events in an interval. Learn the stories and the right formula leaps out before you finish reading the stem.

sections.title: Each distribution answers one question
sections.body: **Binomial**: how many successes in $n$ fixed independent trials? **Geometric**: how many trials until the first success? **Negative binomial**: until the $r$-th success? **Poisson**: how many rare events in a fixed interval, given an average rate? **Hypergeometric**: like binomial but drawing *without* replacement from a finite pool. Match the question to the story first; reach for the formula second.

sections.title: The families and their moments
sections.body: Binomial$(n,p)$: $P(X=k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, mean $np$, variance $np(1-p)$. Geometric$(p)$ (trials until first success): $P(X=k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p$, mean $1/p$, variance $(1-p)/p^2$. Poisson$(\lambda)$: $P(X=k) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$, mean and variance both $\lambda$.

sections.title: Poisson for a call center
sections.body: Calls arrive at a mean rate of 3 per minute. Find the probability of exactly 5 calls in one minute.
steps: This is counting rare-ish events in a fixed interval with a known rate → Poisson with $\lambda = 3$.
$\approx \dfrac{0.0498 \cdot 243}{120} \approx 0.1008$.

sections.title: Binomial recognition and 'at least'
sections.body: A student guesses on a 10-question multiple-choice quiz, each question correct with probability $0.25$ independently. Find the probability of **at least 2** correct, plus the mean and standard deviation of the score.
steps: Identify the story: a *fixed* number of independent trials ($n=10$) with constant success probability ($p=0.25$), counting successes → Binomial$(10, 0.25)$.
'At least 2' is cheapest via the complement: $P(X\ge 2) = 1 - P(X=0) - P(X=1)$.

Moments straight from the formulas: mean $= np = 10(0.25) = 2.5$; variance $= np(1-p) = 10(0.25)(0.75) = 1.875$, so SD $= \sqrt{1.875} \approx 1.37$. (Mean $\ne$ variance here — that rules out Poisson and confirms binomial.)

sections.title: Poisson's signature: mean equals variance
sections.body: If a problem hands you a mean and a variance that are *equal*, suspect Poisson immediately. Also: a binomial with large $n$ and small $p$ is well-approximated by Poisson with $\lambda = np$ — handy when $n$ is too big to compute $\binom{n}{k}$ comfortably.

sections.title: Geometric indexing and the binomial coefficient
sections.body: Two classic slips: (1) the geometric can be indexed as *trials until success* (support $1,2,3,\dots$, mean $1/p$) or *failures before success* (support $0,1,2,\dots$, mean $(1-p)/p$) — read which the problem wants. (2) Binomial needs the $\binom{n}{k}$ coefficient; dropping it counts only one specific ordering of successes, undercounting badly.

cards.front: Why identify the *story* before reaching for a discrete formula?
cards.back: Each family answers a distinct counting question: binomial counts successes in a *fixed* number of trials; geometric/negative-binomial count *trials until* the 1st/$r$-th success; Poisson counts rare events in an interval at a known rate; hypergeometric is binomial *without replacement*. The stem's structure ('how many in $n$' vs 'how long until' vs 'with/without replacement') picks the family — then the formula and moments are automatic.

cards.front: Why does the Poisson have mean = variance, and when does it approximate the binomial?
cards.back: Both equal $\lambda$, so seeing an equal mean and variance is the Poisson fingerprint. It arises as the limit of Binomial$(n,p)$ when $n$ is large and $p$ small with $\lambda = np$ held fixed: the binomial's variance $np(1-p)\to np=\lambda$ as $p\to 0$, collapsing mean and variance together. That makes Poisson$(\lambda=np)$ a fast stand-in when $n$ is too big for $\binom{n}{k}$.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability of exactly two 6's?
Accidents occur at a mean of 2 per week (Poisson). Find $P(\text{no accidents in a week})$.
A salesperson closes each call with probability 0.25, independently. What is the probability the first sale is on the 4th call?
$X \sim$ Poisson with $P(X=1) = P(X=2)$. Find $\lambda$.
In 20 independent trials with success probability 0.1, what are the mean and variance of the number of successes?

concepts.title: The Continuous Families
concepts.tagline: Uniform, exponential, normal, gamma. The exponential's memorylessness and the normal's empirical rule are exam gold.

sections.body: Continuous distributions carry two of the highest-yield tricks on the exam: the exponential's **memorylessness** (the past does not matter) and the normal's **standardization** (every normal question becomes one $Z$-table lookup). These come up again and again — make them reflexes.

sections.title: Three shapes you must recognize on sight
sections.body: **Uniform**: flat — every value in $[a,b]$ equally likely. **Exponential**: waiting time for a Poisson event; a memoryless decay from a peak at 0. **Normal**: the symmetric bell, the limit that the CLT funnels everything toward. If you can sketch these three from memory and know roughly where their mass sits, most continuous questions are half-solved before any algebra.

sections.title: Densities and moments
sections.body: Uniform$(a,b)$: $f(x) = \frac{1}{b-a}$, mean $\frac{a+b}{2}$, variance $\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$. Exponential$(\lambda)$: $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$, mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/\lambda^2$. Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$: standardize with $Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$, then use the standard table.

sections.title: Exponential memorylessness
sections.body: A component's lifetime is exponential with mean 5 years. Given it has already lasted 3 years, find the probability it lasts at least 2 more.
steps: $\lambda = 1/5$. Memorylessness: $P(X > 3+2 \mid X > 3) = P(X > 2)$ — the 3 years are forgotten.
$\approx e^{-0.4} \approx 0.670$.

sections.title: Normal standardization with the Z-table
sections.body: Claim sizes are Normal with mean $\mu = 1000$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 200$. Find $P(X > 1300)$ and $P(900 < X < 1300)$.
steps: Convert each raw value to a $Z$-score by *how many SDs it sits from the mean*: $Z = \dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ — divide by $\sigma = 200$, never by the variance $40{,}000$.
Probability between them is the difference of CDFs: $P(900<X<1300) = \Phi(1.5) - \Phi(-0.5) = 0.9332 - 0.3085 = 0.6247$.
Sanity check against the empirical rule: $1300$ is $1.5$ SD above the mean (upper tail a few percent) and $900$ is $0.5$ SD below — a middle chunk around 62% is exactly what you'd expect. ✓

sections.title: Memorylessness kills the conditioning
sections.body: For an exponential, $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$ — always. The moment you see *given it has already survived...*, drop the elapsed time entirely and compute the fresh tail probability. And for the normal, the empirical rule (68–95–99.7 within 1–2–3 SDs) lets you eyeball many answers without a table.

sections.title: Rate vs mean, and continuity of the normal
sections.body: The exponential's $\lambda$ is a **rate**; its mean is $1/\lambda$. A mean lifetime of 5 means $\lambda = 0.2$, not 5. Mixing these inverts your exponents. Also: when standardizing, divide by $\sigma$ (the SD), not $\sigma^2$ (the variance) — a frequent, costly slip.

cards.front: Why is the exponential memoryless — where does the elapsed time go?
cards.back: Its survival function is $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$, which multiplies: $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=\dfrac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}=e^{-\lambda t}=P(X>t)$. The already-survived time $s$ cancels exactly, so a used component is *as good as new*. That is why 'given it has lasted $s$' lets you discard $s$ and compute a fresh tail.

cards.front: Why standardize a normal by $\sigma$ (not $\sigma^2$), and what does $Z$ measure?
cards.back: $Z = \frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ rescales the variable to *how many standard deviations* it lies from the mean — a pure, unitless distance. That only works if you divide by the SD, which shares $X$'s units; dividing by the variance $\sigma^2$ leaves the wrong units and a wrong $Z$. Once in $Z$ units, every normal collapses to the single standard table.

questions.q: $X$ is uniform on $[2, 10]$. Find $P(X > 7)$.
Lifetimes are exponential with mean 4. Find $P(X > 6)$.
An exponential machine has mean time-to-failure 10 hours. Given it has run 8 hours, find $P(\text{lasts} \ge 5 \text{ more})$.
questions.explain: Memorylessness: the 8 hours vanish, so $P(X>5) = e^{-5/10} = e^{-0.5} \approx 0.607$.

questions.q: $X$ is uniform on $[0, 6]$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

concepts.title: Moment Generating Functions
concepts.tagline: One function that encodes every moment, identifies the distribution, and turns sums into products. The MGF is the Swiss-army knife of Exam P.

sections.body: Imagine a single function that, when you take its derivatives at zero, hands you the mean, the variance, the third moment — every moment, on demand. That is the **moment generating function**, and the exam loves it because it also *uniquely fingerprints* a distribution and collapses the sum of independent variables into a simple product. Master the MGF and a whole class of questions becomes mechanical.

sections.title: Why differentiating at zero pulls out moments
sections.body: The MGF is $M(t) = E[e^{tX}]$. Expand $e^{tX} = 1 + tX + \frac{t^2X^2}{2!} + \frac{t^3X^3}{3!} + \cdots$ and take expectations: $M(t) = 1 + tE[X] + \frac{t^2}{2!}E[X^2] + \cdots$. The coefficient of $t^k$ is $E[X^k]/k!$, so the $k$-th derivative at $t=0$ peels off exactly $E[X^k]$. The MGF is a power series whose coefficients *are* the moments — differentiation is just reading off the term you want.

sections.title: The three properties you will actually use
sections.body: **Moments:** $E[X^k] = M^{(k)}(0)$. So $E[X] = M'(0)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = M''(0) - [M'(0)]^2$. **Uniqueness:** if two variables have the same MGF on an interval around 0, they have the same distribution — match the MGF to a known form to identify it. **Independent sums:** if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)\,M_Y(t)$; and $M_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt}M_X(at)$.

sections.title: Reading moments off an MGF
sections.body: A random variable has $M(t) = (1 - 250t)^{-4}$ for $t < 1/250$. Find its mean and variance.
steps: (This is a Gamma with shape 4, scale 250: mean $= 4\cdot250 = 1000$, variance $= 4\cdot250^2 = 250\,000$ — the MGF identified it.)

sections.title: Turning a sum of independents into a product
sections.body: $X \sim \text{Normal}(2, 9)$ and $Y \sim \text{Normal}(1, 16)$ are independent. Use MGFs to find the distribution of $X + Y$.
steps: Write each MGF from the normal form $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$: $M_X(t) = e^{2t + 9t^2/2}$ and $M_Y(t) = e^{t + 16t^2/2}$.
Independence means the sum's MGF is the *product*: $M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)\,M_Y(t) = e^{(2+1)t + (9+16)t^2/2} = e^{3t + 25t^2/2}$.
Pattern-match the result back to $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$: $\mu = 3$, $\sigma^2 = 25$. By uniqueness, $X+Y \sim \text{Normal}(3, 25)$.
Cross-check: for independent variables means add ($2+1=3$) and variances add ($9+16=25$). The MGF does more — it *proves the sum is still normal*, not merely that the first two moments add. ✓

sections.title: Match the form, skip the calculus
sections.body: Memorize the canonical MGFs and you often never differentiate. Poisson$(\lambda)$: $e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$. Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$: $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$. Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$: $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$. Exponential$(\lambda)$ is Gamma with $\alpha=1$: $(1-t/\lambda)^{-1} = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}$. When an MGF appears, try to read off its parameters by pattern-matching — then quote the mean and variance from memory.

sections.title: Subtract the square, and respect the $e^{bt}$ shift
sections.body: $M''(0)$ gives $E[X^2]$, **not** the variance — you still subtract $[M'(0)]^2$. Forgetting this is the single most common MGF error. Second trap: for a linear transform $aX+b$, the MGF is $e^{bt}M_X(at)$, with the constant riding *outside* as $e^{bt}$ and the scale going *inside* the argument — do not multiply $M_X$ by $a$.

cards.front: Why does the $k$-th derivative of $M(t)$ at $0$ produce $E[X^k]$ — and why must you still subtract for variance?
cards.back: Expanding $M(t)=E[e^{tX}] = 1 + tE[X] + \frac{t^2}{2!}E[X^2] + \cdots$ makes the coefficient of $t^k$ equal $E[X^k]/k!$, so differentiating $k$ times and setting $t=0$ isolates $E[X^k]$. But $M''(0)=E[X^2]$ is the *raw* second moment, so variance still needs $M''(0) - [M'(0)]^2$ — forgetting that subtraction is the classic MGF error.

cards.front: Why does an independent sum multiply MGFs, and what does the uniqueness property buy you?
cards.back: $M_{X+Y}(t)=E[e^{t(X+Y)}]=E[e^{tX}e^{tY}]$, and independence factors the expectation into $M_X(t)M_Y(t)$. Uniqueness says an MGF fingerprints exactly one distribution, so after multiplying you can pattern-match the product to a known form and *identify* the sum's distribution — proving, e.g., that independent normals sum to a normal, not just that their moments add.

questions.q: $M(t) = e^{3t + 8t^2}$. What are the mean and variance of $X$?
$X$ has MGF $M(t) = \frac{1}{1-2t}$ for $t < 1/2$. Find $E[X^2]$.
$X$ and $Y$ are independent with $M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$ and $M_Y(t) = e^{\mu(e^t-1)}$. The distribution of $X+Y$ is:
If $M_X(t) = (1-3t)^{-2}$, find the MGF of $Y = 2X + 1$.
$M(t) = 0.3 + 0.7e^t$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

concepts.title: Transformations of a Random Variable
concepts.tagline: Given the distribution of $X$, find the distribution of $Y=g(X)$. The CDF method always works; the Jacobian shortcut is faster when $g$ is monotone.

sections.body: The exam rarely hands you the variable you want. It gives you $X$ and asks about $Y = X^2$, or $Y = e^X$, or $Y = \sqrt{X}$. There is one method that *never* fails — go through the CDF — and one shortcut that is faster when the transform is one-to-one. Knowing which to reach for is the whole game.

sections.title: Chase the probability through the CDF
sections.body: A transformation reshapes the density, but probabilities of *events* are preserved. So translate the question about $Y$ into an equivalent question about $X$: $F_Y(y) = P(Y \le y) = P(g(X) \le y)$. Solve the inequality for $X$, evaluate using the known CDF of $X$, then differentiate to get the density of $Y$. You are simply following the same probability mass to its new location on the $y$-axis.

sections.title: CDF method and the Jacobian shortcut
sections.body: **CDF method (always works):** $F_Y(y) = P(g(X)\le y)$; differentiate to get $f_Y(y)$. **Jacobian (monotone $g$ only):** if $y=g(x)$ is one-to-one with inverse $x = g^{-1}(y)$, then $f_Y(y) = f_X\!\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|$. The absolute value of the derivative is the **Jacobian** — it rescales the density so total area stays 1.

sections.title: A non-monotone transform: $Y = X^2$
sections.body: Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1)$, so $f_X(x) = \tfrac12$ on $[-1,1]$. Find the density of $Y = X^2$.
steps: $g(x)=x^2$ is **not** monotone on $[-1,1]$, so use the CDF method. For $0 \le y \le 1$: $F_Y(y) = P(X^2 \le y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \le X \le \sqrt{y})$.
$= \int_{-\sqrt{y}}^{\sqrt{y}} \tfrac12\,dx = \tfrac12\,(2\sqrt{y}) = \sqrt{y}$.
Differentiate: $f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy}\sqrt{y} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$ for $0 < y < 1$.
Note the density blows up near 0 and the support collapsed to $[0,1]$ — exactly why you cannot just plug into the Jacobian formula here.

sections.title: A monotone transform via the Jacobian
sections.body: Let $X \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$, so $f_X(x) = e^{-x}$ for $x > 0$. Find the density of $Y = \sqrt{X}$.
steps: Here $g(x)=\sqrt{x}$ *is* monotone increasing on $x>0$, so the Jacobian shortcut applies. Invert: $x = g^{-1}(y) = y^2$.
Jacobian (the stretch factor): $\dfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{d}{dy}y^2 = 2y$, and $|2y| = 2y$ for $y>0$.
Assemble: $f_Y(y) = f_X(y^2)\,|2y| = e^{-y^2}\cdot 2y = 2y\,e^{-y^2}$ for $y>0$ (a Rayleigh density).

Update the support and cross-check it integrates to 1: $x>0 \Rightarrow y>0$, and $\int_0^\infty 2y\,e^{-y^2}\,dy = \big[-e^{-y^2}\big]_0^\infty = 1$. ✓ The Jacobian rescaled the density so the total area is preserved.

sections.title: Probability integral transform
sections.body: Two universal facts the exam exploits: (1) If $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ then $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$ — this is how you *simulate* any distribution. (2) Going the other way, if $X$ has continuous CDF $F$, then $F(X) \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. So a transform like $Y = 1 - e^{-\lambda X}$ applied to an exponential is *exactly* its own CDF, making $Y$ uniform on $(0,1)$ instantly — no integration needed.

sections.title: Monotonicity and the new support
sections.body: Never apply the Jacobian formula to a non-monotone $g$ (like $x^2$ over a symmetric interval) — you will miss half the probability. When $g$ folds the line, split into monotone pieces or use the CDF method. Second trap: always restate the **support** of $Y$. The range of $g$ over the support of $X$ sets where $f_Y$ is nonzero; forgetting to update it produces a density that does not integrate to 1.

cards.front: Why does the CDF method work for *any* transform when the Jacobian doesn't?
cards.back: Events keep their probability even after $g$ reshapes the density, so $F_Y(y)=P(g(X)\le y)$ just rewrites the question in terms of $X$, solves the inequality, and reads off the known $F_X$ — then differentiate for $f_Y$. It never assumes $g$ is one-to-one, so it handles folds like $x^2$ that map two $x$'s to one $y$, where the Jacobian would silently miss half the mass.

cards.front: What does the Jacobian $|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)|$ do, and why must you restate the support of $Y$?
cards.back: For a monotone $g$ the Jacobian is the local stretch factor: it rescales $f_X$ so that probability is conserved when the axis is stretched or compressed, keeping the total area at 1. You must also map the support — the range of $g$ over $X$'s support sets where $f_Y$ is nonzero; skip that and the 'density' won't integrate to 1.

questions.q: $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and $Y = -\ln X$. The distribution of $Y$ is:
questions.explain: $F_Y(y)=P(-\ln X\le y)=P(X\ge e^{-y})=1-e^{-y}$ for $y>0$ — exponential, rate 1, mean 1.

questions.q: $X$ has density $f_X(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$. Let $Y=X^2$. Find $f_Y(y)$ on $(0,1)$.
$X\sim\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$. The distribution of $Y=1-e^{-\lambda X}$ is:
questions.explain: $1-e^{-\lambda x}$ is the exponential CDF, so $Y=F(X)\sim$ Uniform$(0,1)$ by the probability integral transform.

questions.q: $X\sim N(0,1)$ and $Y=e^{X}$. The variable $Y$ is called:
questions.explain: By definition, the exponential of a normal is lognormal.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Uniform}(0,2)$ and $Y=3X+1$. The density $f_Y(y)$ is constant equal to:
questions.explain: Linear monotone transform: $Y$ is uniform on $(1,7)$, length 6, so $f_Y=\frac16$.

concepts.title: Percentiles, Median & Mode
concepts.tagline: Beyond the mean: how to find the value at a given probability, where the density peaks, and why skew separates the three centers.

sections.body: The mean is one summary of a distribution — but the exam also asks for the **median** (the 50th percentile), the **mode** (the most likely value), and arbitrary **percentiles** ('the value-at-risk such that only 5% exceeds it'). Each answers a different question, and in a skewed distribution they pull apart in a predictable order you can exploit.

sections.title: Three different notions of 'center'
sections.body: The **median** splits the area under the density in half — half the probability lies on each side. The **mode** is where the density is tallest — the most likely neighborhood. The **mean** is the balance point, the center of mass. For a symmetric distribution all three coincide. Skew the distribution and they spread out: a long right tail drags the mean above the median, which sits above the mode.

sections.title: Finding each one
sections.body: **$p$-th percentile** $\pi_p$: solve $F(\pi_p) = p$. **Median** $m$: solve $F(m) = 0.5$. **Mode**: maximize $f(x)$ — for a differentiable density, solve $f'(x)=0$ and check it is a maximum. For the exponential$(\lambda)$, setting $1-e^{-\lambda \pi_p} = p$ gives $\pi_p = -\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1-p)$, so the median is $\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.

sections.title: Percentile of an exponential
sections.body: Claim sizes are exponential with mean 500. Find the 90th percentile (the value exceeded only 10% of the time).
steps: So 90% of claims fall below about 1151 — a useful 'value-at-risk' style figure.

sections.title: Mean vs median vs mode on a skewed density
sections.body: A variable has density $f(x) = 2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ (it slopes down from a peak at the left). Find the mode, median, and mean, and confirm how they line up.
steps: **Mode** — where the density is tallest: $f(x)=2(1-x)$ decreases across $[0,1]$, so its maximum is at the left edge, $x = 0$. Mode $= 0$.
**Median** — splits the area in half. CDF: $F(x)=\int_0^x 2(1-t)\,dt = 2x - x^2$. Set $2m - m^2 = 0.5 \Rightarrow m^2 - 2m + 0.5 = 0 \Rightarrow m = 1 - \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 0.293$.
**Mean** — the balance point: $E[X]=\int_0^1 x\cdot 2(1-x)\,dx = \int_0^1 (2x - 2x^2)\,dx = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$.
Line them up: mode $0 <$ median $0.293 <$ mean $0.333$. The long right tail pulls the mean highest — exactly the right-skew ordering mode $<$ median $<$ mean. ✓

sections.title: Mean > median > mode for right skew
sections.body: For a right-skewed distribution (long upper tail — lognormal, exponential, most loss models), the ordering is **mean $>$ median $>$ mode**. The rare large values inflate the mean most, the median less, and leave the mode (the peak) alone. If a question shows mean far above median, you are looking at right skew — and the mean is *not* a typical value. This single fact answers many qualitative questions instantly.

sections.title: Percentile means the value, not the probability
sections.body: The $p$-th percentile is the **$x$-value** $\pi_p$ such that $F(\pi_p)=p$ — not the probability $p$ itself. Students sometimes report 0.90 when asked for the 90th percentile; the answer is the dollar/time amount. Also: for discrete or mixed distributions the percentile may not be unique (a flat stretch of the CDF), and the median is the conventional choice in that interval.

cards.front: What exactly is the $p$-th percentile — and what's the classic wrong answer?
cards.back: It's the *$x$-value* $\pi_p$ at which the accumulated probability reaches $p$: solve $F(\pi_p)=p$. The classic slip is reporting $p$ itself (e.g. 0.90) when asked for the 90th percentile — the answer is the dollar/time/loss amount $\pi_p$, not the probability.

cards.front: Why do mean, median, and mode coincide when symmetric but separate under skew?
cards.back: Each measures a different 'center': median halves the area, mode is the density's peak, mean is the balance point. Symmetry makes all three land at the axis of symmetry. A long right tail adds rare large values that pull the *balance point* (mean) outward most, the area-splitting median less, and leave the peak (mode) put — giving mode $<$ median $<$ mean for right skew (reversed for left).

questions.q: Losses are exponential with mean 1000. Find the median.
questions.explain: Median $=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}=1000\ln 2\approx 693$. Note it is below the mean — right skew.

questions.q: $X$ has CDF $F(x)=x^3$ on $(0,1)$. Find the 25th percentile.
A distribution is right-skewed. Which ordering holds?
questions.explain: Right skew (long upper tail) drags the mean highest: mean $>$ median $>$ mode.

questions.q: $X$ has density $f(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$. Find the mode.
questions.explain: $f(x)=2x$ increases on $(0,1)$, so the density is tallest at the right endpoint $x=1$.

questions.q: For a symmetric, unimodal distribution, the median equals:
choices: both the mean and the mode
questions.explain: Symmetry forces all three measures of center to coincide.

concepts.title: Gamma, Beta & Lognormal
concepts.tagline: The three advanced continuous families the exam expects you to recognize: waiting-time sums, bounded proportions, and multiplicative growth.

sections.body: Once you are past uniform, exponential, and normal, three more families show up with real frequency — and each has a *story* that tells you when it appears. **Gamma** is the wait for several Poisson events. **Beta** lives on $[0,1]$ and models proportions. **Lognormal** is what you get when effects multiply instead of add. Recognize the story and you have already picked the distribution.

sections.title: Each family's origin story
sections.body: **Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$**: add $\alpha$ independent exponentials with mean $\theta$ and you get a Gamma — the total time to the $\alpha$-th arrival. Shape $\alpha$ controls how bell-like it becomes. **Beta$(\alpha,\beta)$**: the natural distribution for a random *fraction* — flexible shapes on $[0,1]$, the conjugate prior for a binomial proportion. **Lognormal**: if $\ln X$ is normal, $X$ is lognormal — the limit of many *multiplicative* shocks, so it models asset prices and loss sizes with a long right tail.

sections.title: Moments worth memorizing
sections.body: **Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$**: mean $\alpha\theta$, variance $\alpha\theta^2$, MGF $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$. **Beta$(\alpha,\beta)$**: mean $\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}$, variance $\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}$. **Lognormal**: if $\ln X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then $E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = e^{2\mu+\sigma^2}\big(e^{\sigma^2}-1\big)$. Probabilities for the lognormal are done by taking logs and using the normal table.

sections.title: A lognormal probability
sections.body: Annual losses $X$ are lognormal with $\mu = 7$ and $\sigma = 2$. Find $P(X > 1000)$, given $\Phi(0.05) = 0.520$.
steps: Take logs: $P(X > 1000) = P(\ln X > \ln 1000)$, and $\ln 1000 \approx 6.908$.
So there is about a 52% chance the annual loss exceeds 1000.

sections.title: Gamma as a sum of waits
sections.body: Claims arrive in a Poisson process; the time between successive claims is exponential with mean $\theta = 2$ hours. Find the mean and standard deviation of the waiting time until the **4th** claim, and name the distribution.
steps: The 4th-arrival time is the sum of 4 independent exponential waits, which is exactly Gamma$(\alpha, \theta) = \text{Gamma}(4, 2)$ — that is the Gamma's origin story.
Mean straight from the formula: $E[X] = \alpha\theta = 4(2) = 8$ hours.
Variance: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = \alpha\theta^2 = 4(2^2) = 16$, so SD $= 4$ hours.

Cross-check via the sum: each exponential has mean $2$ and variance $\theta^2 = 4$; for independent variables means and variances add, giving mean $4(2)=8$ and variance $4(4)=16$. ✓ Same answer, confirming Gamma is just stacked exponentials.

sections.title: Take logs first for anything lognormal
sections.body: Every lognormal *probability* question reduces to a normal one: turn $X$ into $\ln X$, standardize, hit the $Z$-table. Never integrate the lognormal density. And for the Gamma, remember it is just a sum of exponentials — if you see 'time until the 3rd claim' with exponential interarrivals, that total is Gamma$(3,\theta)$ and you can quote mean $3\theta$ and variance $3\theta^2$ without setup.

sections.title: Lognormal mean is not $e^{\mu}$
sections.body: The most punished lognormal error: $E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$, **not** $e^{\mu}$. The quantity $e^{\mu}$ is the *median* of the lognormal; the mean is larger because of the right skew. Forgetting the $+\sigma^2/2$ understates the mean every time. Separately, for the Gamma, $\theta$ is the **scale** (so variance carries $\theta^2$); some texts use rate $\beta = 1/\theta$ — check which convention a problem uses.

cards.front: How does each family's *story* tell you to pick it on sight?
cards.back: Gamma is the *sum of $\alpha$ exponential waits* — use it for 'time until the $\alpha$-th event' (mean $\alpha\theta$, variance $\alpha\theta^2$). Beta lives on $[0,1]$ — use it for a random *proportion or fraction*. Lognormal is what you get when many effects *multiply* (so $\ln X$ is normal) — use it for asset prices and loss sizes with a long right tail. Match the mechanism, then quote the moments.

cards.front: Why is the lognormal mean $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$ rather than $e^\mu$, and how do you get its probabilities?
cards.back: $e^\mu$ is the *median* (the point where $\ln X = \mu$); the right skew drags the mean above it by the factor $e^{\sigma^2/2}$, so $E[X]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$ — dropping that term understates the mean every time. For any lognormal *probability*, don't integrate the density: take logs to convert to $\ln X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, standardize, and read the normal table.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Gamma}(3, 4)$ (shape 3, scale 4). Find its mean and variance.
$\ln X \sim N(0, 1)$. Find $E[X]$.
$X\sim\text{Beta}(2, 3)$. Find $E[X]$.
Interarrival times are exponential with mean 2. The time until the 4th arrival has which distribution?
questions.explain: Sum of 4 independent Exponential(mean 2) is Gamma with shape 4, scale 2.

questions.q: For a lognormal with $\ln X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the median equals:
questions.explain: The median is $e^{\mu}$ (since the median of $\ln X$ is $\mu$); the mean is the larger $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$.

modules.title: Multivariate Random Variables
modules.blurb: Two or more variables at once: joint and marginal distributions, covariance and correlation, conditional expectation, sums of random variables, and the Central Limit Theorem that ties the whole exam together.

concepts.title: Joint & Marginal Distributions
concepts.tagline: Two variables share one probability surface. Marginalizing is just summing or integrating out the variable you stopped caring about.

sections.body: When two random variables interact — a loss and its deductible, a claim count and its severity — they share **one joint distribution**, a surface of probability over a plane. Reading that surface (and collapsing it back to one variable) is the core skill of the final module.

sections.title: Marginalize = sum out what you ignore
sections.body: The **joint** $f(x,y)$ is the full surface. To get the **marginal** of $X$ alone, you collapse the surface along the $Y$ direction — sum (discrete) or integrate (continuous) over all $y$. You are pooling together every way $X = x$ could happen, regardless of $Y$. The word *marginal* is literal: old textbooks wrote these sums in the margins.

sections.title: Marginals, independence, and joint expectation
sections.body: Marginal: $f_X(x) = \int f(x,y)\,dy$ (or $\sum_y$). Independence holds iff the joint factors: $f(x,y) = f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)$ for all $x,y$. Expectation of a function: $$E[g(X,Y)] = \iint g(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$$

sections.title: Marginal from a joint density
sections.body: Let $f(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square $0 \le x,y \le 1$. Find the marginal $f_X(x)$.
steps: Integrate out $y$ over $[0,1]$: $f_X(x) = \int_0^1 (x + y)\,dy$.
Valid for $0 \le x \le 1$.

sections.title: Test independence by trying to factor
sections.body: To check independence fast, see whether $f(x,y)$ splits into a pure-$x$ piece times a pure-$y$ piece **over a rectangular region**. If the support is a triangle, or the density tangles $x$ and $y$ together (like $x + y$), they are dependent — no need to compute marginals first.

sections.title: Ignoring the region of support
sections.body: The limits of integration come from the **support**, not always $0$ to $1$. If $X$ and $Y$ live on a triangle like $0 < x < y < 1$, the marginal of $X$ integrates $y$ from $x$ to $1$, not $0$ to $1$. Getting the bounds wrong silently corrupts every downstream answer — sketch the region first.

cards.front: How do you get $f_X(x)$ from a joint density?
cards.back: Integrate (or sum) the joint over all values of $y$ — collapse the surface along $Y$.

cards.front: Independence test for a joint density?
cards.back: It factors as $f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ over a rectangular support; tangled densities or non-rectangular support mean dependence.

cards.front: What sets the integration limits for a marginal?
cards.back: The region of support of the joint distribution — sketch it first.

questions.q: For $f(x,y) = x+y$ on the unit square, find $E[X]$.
$X$ and $Y$ have joint pmf with $P(0,0)=0.1, P(0,1)=0.2, P(1,0)=0.3, P(1,1)=0.4$. Find the marginal $P(X=1)$.
A joint density is $f(x,y) = 4xy$ on the unit square. Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?
choices: No, the support is a triangle
questions.explain: Over the rectangular unit square, $4xy = (2x)(2y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$, so $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

questions.q: For $f(x,y) = 2$ on $0 < x < y < 1$, find the marginal $f_Y(y)$.

concepts.title: Covariance & Correlation
concepts.tagline: How two variables move together — and the formula for the variance of a sum that the exam asks for relentlessly.

sections.body: Covariance measures whether two variables rise and fall together. Its single most-tested consequence: the **variance of a sum** picks up a covariance term. Forget that term and you will systematically miss portfolio and aggregate-loss questions worth real points.

sections.title: Do they move together or against?
sections.body: Positive covariance: when $X$ is above its mean, $Y$ tends to be too — they move *together*. Negative: they move *oppositely*. Zero: no linear relationship. Correlation is just covariance rescaled to $[-1, 1]$ so you can compare across different units — it strips out the magnitudes and keeps only the direction and tightness of the linear link.

sections.title: Covariance, correlation, variance of a sum
sections.body: $$\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$$ $$\rho = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}, \quad -1 \le \rho \le 1$$ The headline result: $$\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$$

sections.title: Variance of a sum with covariance
sections.body: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 9$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = 2$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X + Y)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X - Y)$.
steps: For a difference the covariance term flips sign: $\mathrm{Var}(X-Y) = 4 + 9 - 2(2) = 9$.
Note both exceed neither variance alone — covariance shifts them apart.

sections.title: Independent → covariance is 0 → variances just add
sections.body: If the problem says independent (or uncorrelated), $\mathrm{Cov} = 0$, so $\mathrm{Var}(X \pm Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)$ — note it is a **plus** even for a difference, because the covariance term that would carry the sign is zero. That subtlety trips up a lot of students.

sections.title: Zero correlation does not mean independent
sections.body: $\rho = 0$ rules out a *linear* relationship, but variables can be strongly dependent in a nonlinear way and still have zero covariance (e.g. $Y = X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about 0). Independence implies zero covariance; the reverse is false. Do not upgrade *uncorrelated* to *independent*.

cards.front: $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = ?$ in terms of expectations.
cards.back: $E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$.

cards.front: $\mathrm{Var}(X - Y)$ for correlated variables?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) - 2\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$ — the covariance term flips to minus.

cards.front: Does $\rho = 0$ imply independence?
cards.back: No — only no linear relationship. Independence implies $\rho=0$, not the reverse.

questions.q: $E[XY] = 10$, $E[X] = 3$, $E[Y] = 2$. Find $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$.
$\mathrm{Var}(X)=5$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=8$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=-2$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)$.
Two uncorrelated risks each have variance 16. What is the standard deviation of their total?
$X$ and $Y$ have $\sigma_X = 2$, $\sigma_Y = 5$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = 4$. Find the correlation $\rho$.
A portfolio is $W = 2X + 3Y$ with $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=2$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0.5$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(W)$.

concepts.title: Conditional Distributions
concepts.tagline: Once you learn $Y=y$, the distribution of $X$ updates. Slice the joint surface, renormalize, and you have the conditional density.

sections.body: Information changes probability. The instant you learn that a policyholder filed exactly two claims, the distribution of their *total loss* shifts. The machinery for that update — slicing the joint distribution and rescaling it — is the **conditional distribution**, and it underpins every credibility, mixture, and double-expectation question on the exam.

sections.title: A conditional density is a renormalized slice
sections.body: Picture the joint surface $f(x,y)$. Fixing $Y = y$ takes a single vertical slice through it. That slice has the right *shape* for the distribution of $X$ given $Y=y$, but its area is only $f_Y(y)$, not 1. Divide by $f_Y(y)$ to rescale the slice back to a legitimate density. That is all a conditional density is: a slice, renormalized so it integrates to 1.

sections.title: Conditional density and expectation
sections.body: $$f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}$$ The conditional expectation is the mean of that slice: $$E[X \mid Y=y] = \int x\,f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx$$ If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, conditioning changes nothing: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = f_X(x)$.

sections.title: Conditional density from a joint
sections.body: Let $f(x,y) = \frac{x+y}{?}$… use $f(x,y) = 2$ on the triangle $0 < x < y < 1$. Find $f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid y)$ and $E[X \mid Y = y]$.
steps: Marginal of $Y$: $f_Y(y) = \int_0^y 2\,dx = 2y$ for $0 < y < 1$.
Conditional: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = \frac{2}{2y} = \frac{1}{y}$ for $0 < x < y$ — i.e. $X \mid Y=y$ is Uniform$(0,y)$.
So $E[X \mid Y=y] = \frac{y}{2}$ (mean of a uniform on $(0,y)$).
The conditional turned a 2-D triangle into a simple 1-D uniform once $y$ is fixed.

sections.title: Recognize the slice as a named distribution
sections.body: After you divide by the marginal, the conditional density is often a *standard* distribution in disguise — uniform, exponential, beta. The moment you recognize it (as Uniform$(0,y)$ above), you can quote its mean and variance instead of integrating. This shortcut is enormous in double-expectation problems, where you need $E[X\mid Y]$ as a function of $Y$.

sections.title: Divide by the right marginal, and keep the support
sections.body: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ divides by $f_Y(y)$ — the marginal of the variable you *conditioned on*, not the one you want. Swapping them is a classic error. And the conditional's support depends on $y$: above, $X$ ranges only over $(0,y)$, not $(0,1)$. Carrying the wrong support breaks the normalization and every expectation after it.

cards.front: Conditional density formula?
cards.back: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}$ — slice over marginal.

cards.front: What is $E[X\mid Y=y]$?
cards.back: The mean of the conditional distribution — a function of $y$.

cards.front: Conditional when $X,Y$ independent?
cards.back: Just the marginal: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=f_X(x)$.

cards.front: Why divide by the marginal?
cards.back: To renormalize the slice (area $f_Y(y)$) back to a density of total area 1.

questions.q: $f(x,y)=2$ on $0<x<y<1$. Find $E[X\mid Y=0.6]$.
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ equals:
questions.explain: Independence means conditioning adds no information: the conditional is just the marginal $f_X(x)$.

questions.q: Joint pmf: $P(X{=}1,Y{=}1)=0.2$, and the marginal $P(Y{=}1)=0.5$. Find $P(X{=}1\mid Y{=}1)$.
$X\mid Y=y$ is exponential with mean $y$. Find $E[X\mid Y=4]$.
questions.explain: An exponential with mean $y$ has $E[X\mid Y=y]=y$, so $E[X\mid Y=4]=4$.

questions.q: $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}$ for $0<x<y<1$ describes $X\mid Y=y$ as:
questions.explain: Constant density $1/y$ on $(0,y)$ is the Uniform$(0,y)$ distribution.

concepts.title: Double Expectation & the Variance Decomposition
concepts.tagline: $E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\mathrm{Var}(E[X\mid Y])$ — the two laws that crack every mixture problem.

sections.body: Some of the highest-value questions on Exam P look impossible head-on: a Poisson number of claims, each of random size; a loss whose mean depends on an unknown risk class. The key that unlocks all of them is **conditioning** — solve the easy problem given the hidden variable, then average over it. Two laws make this airtight: the **law of total expectation** and the **law of total variance**.

sections.title: Average the conditional answers
sections.body: If you knew the risk class $Y$, finding $E[X\mid Y]$ would be easy. You do not know $Y$ — so treat $E[X\mid Y]$ as a *random variable* (it depends on which $Y$ you land in) and average it: $E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]$. Variance splits the same way but into **two** pieces: the average spread *within* each class, plus the spread *between* the class means. Total uncertainty = uncertainty inside groups + uncertainty across groups.

sections.title: The two laws
sections.body: **Total expectation:** $$E[X] = E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]$$ **Total variance:** $$\mathrm{Var}(X) = \underbrace{E\big[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)\big]}_{\text{within (expected process var)}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\big(E[X\mid Y]\big)}_{\text{between (variance of hypothetical means)}}$$ In credibility language these are the *expected process variance* and the *variance of the hypothetical means*.

widget.caption: Two risk classes, each with its own mean and spread. Watch how the **total** variance is always the within-class variance plus the between-class variance — and how widening the gap between the class means inflates the 'between' term while leaving the 'within' term untouched.

sections.title: A two-class mixture
sections.body: 70% of drivers are low-risk with mean claim 1 and variance 1; 30% are high-risk with mean claim 4 and variance 9. Find $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ for a randomly chosen driver.

sections.title: Compound sums: $E[S]=E[N]E[X]$
sections.body: For a compound sum $S = X_1 + \dots + X_N$ where $N$ is random and the $X_i$ are iid (mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$), the laws give two memorizable results: $E[S] = E[N]\,\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S) = E[N]\,\sigma^2 + \mu^2\,\mathrm{Var}(N)$. If $N$ is Poisson$(\lambda)$ (so mean = variance = $\lambda$), this collapses to the elegant $\mathrm{Var}(S) = \lambda\,E[X^2]$. Memorize these — they appear every sitting.

sections.title: Don't drop the between-group term
sections.body: The most expensive error in this topic: computing only $E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]$ and calling it the variance. That ignores the variance *between* the conditional means and **understates** total variance. Total variance is always the sum of both pieces. Symmetric warning: $E[X]$ uses only the first law, but $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ needs both — never reuse the expectation shortcut for variance.

cards.front: Law of total expectation?
cards.back: $E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]$ — average the conditional means.

cards.front: Law of total variance?
cards.back: $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\mathrm{Var}(E[X\mid Y])$ (within + between).

cards.front: Compound mean $E[S]$ for $S=\sum_1^N X_i$?
Compound variance $\mathrm{Var}(S)$?
cards.back: $E[N]\mathrm{Var}(X)+(E[X])^2\mathrm{Var}(N)$; Poisson $N$: $\lambda E[X^2]$.

choices: The variance between the group means
